The story effectively presents three distinct perspectives: the observant, slightly insecure narrator; Meredith, a hard-working, pragmatic junior associate from the Midwest; and Quentin ("Q"), an entitled, conflict-averse elitist. 

Although Q is a morally ambiguous and ultimately unappealing character—using charm to manipulate romantic partners and firing a dedicated employee by a beach club pool without even reading her file—his viewpoint is depicted with great accuracy and believability. Rather than portraying him as a cartoonish villain, the narrative convincingly captures his internal logic: a deep-seated aversion to "social friction" and ugliness. When he tells Meredith, "I thought it would be more civilized... I thought we could have a drink, look at the water, and talk like human beings," the reader fully understands his self-delusion and the cowardice masked as grace that motivates his actions.
